{{short description|Mathematical techniques for summing divergent infinite series}}
{{distinguish|Ramanujan's sum}}
{{further|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}}

{{confusing|date=December 2020}}

'''Ramanujan summation''' is a technique invented by the mathematician [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]] for assigning a value to [[divergent series|divergent]] [[infinite series]]. Although the Ramanujan summation of a divergent series is not a sum in the traditional sense, it has properties that make it mathematically useful in the study of divergent [[infinite series]], for which conventional summation is undefined.

== Summation ==

Since there are no properties of an entire sum, the Ramanujan summation functions as a property of partial sums. If we take the [[Euler–Maclaurin formula|Euler–Maclaurin summation formula]] together with the correction rule using [[Bernoulli number]]s, we see that:{{clarify|date=December 2020}}{{Explain|date=December 2020}}
: <math>\begin{align}
\frac 1 2 f(0) + f(1) + \cdots + f(n - 1) + \frac 1 2 f(n) &= \frac {f(0) + f(n)} {2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} f(k) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} f(k) - \frac {f(0) + f(n)} {2} \\
  &= \int_0^n f(x)\,dx + \sum_{k=1}^p \frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!}\left[f^{(2k-1)}(n) - f^{(2k-1)}(0)\right] + R_p
\end{align}</math>

Ramanujan<ref>{{cite book |first=Bruce C. |last=Berndt  |authorlink= Bruce C. Berndt |url=http://www.comms.scitech.susx.ac.uk/fft/math/RamanujanNotebooks1.pdf |title=Ramanujan's Notebooks: Part 1 |chapter=Ramanujan's Theory of Divergent Series |publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=1985 |pages=133–149|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061012064851/http://www.comms.scitech.susx.ac.uk/fft/math/RamanujanNotebooks1.pdf |archive-date=12 October 2006 }}</ref> wrote this again for different limits of the integral and the corresponding summation for the case in which ''p'' goes to [[infinity]]:
: <math>
\sum_{k=a}^{x}f(k)=C+\int_a^x f(t)dt+\frac{1}{2}f(x)+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!}f^{(2k-1)}(x)
</math>
where ''C'' is a constant specific to the series and its [[analytic continuation]] and the limits on the integral were not specified by Ramanujan, but presumably they were as given above. Comparing both formulae and assuming that ''R'' tends to 0 as ''x'' tends to infinity, we see that, in a general case, for functions ''f''(''x'') with no divergence at ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0:
: <math>C(a)=\int_0^a f(t)\,dt - \frac 1 2 f(0)-\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!}f^{(2k-1)}(0)</math>
where Ramanujan assumed {{tmath|1=a = 0}}. By taking <math>a= \infty</math> we normally recover the usual summation for convergent series. For functions ''f''(''x'') with no divergence at {{nowrap|1=''x'' = 1}}, we obtain:
: <math>C(a) = \int_1^a f(t)\,dt+ \frac{1}{2}f(1) - \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!} f^{(2k-1)}(1)</math>
alternatively, applying [[smoothed sums]].

The convergent version of summation for functions with appropriate growth condition is then{{citation needed|date=December 2020}}:
: <math>f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+\cdots=-\frac{f(0)} 2 + i\int_0^\infty \frac{f(it)-f(-it)}{e^{2\pi t}-1} \, dt</math>

{{crossreference|text=To compare, see [[Abel–Plana formula]].|printworthy=yes}}

== Ramanujan summation of divergent series ==

In the following text, <math>(\mathfrak{R})</math> indicates "Ramanujan summation". This formula originally appeared in one of Ramanujan's notebooks, without any notation to indicate that it exemplified a novel method of summation.

For example, the <math>(\mathfrak{R})</math> of {{nowrap|[[Grandi's series|1 − 1 + 1 − ⋯]]}} is:
: <math>1 - 1 + 1 - \cdots = \frac 1 2\quad (\mathfrak{R}).</math>

Ramanujan had calculated "sums" of known divergent series. It is important to mention that the Ramanujan sums are not the sums of the series in the usual sense,<ref name="Terry Tao on Ramanujan sums">{{cite web |title=The Euler–Maclaurin formula, Bernoulli numbers, the zeta function, and real-variable analytic continuation |url=http://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/04/10/the-euler-maclaurin-formula-bernoulli-numbers-the-zeta-function-and-real-variable-analytic-continuation/ |first=Terence |last=Tao |authorlink=Terence Tao |date=10 April 2010 |website=What's new |accessdate=20 January 2014}}</ref><ref name="Dirichlet vs Zeta">{{cite web |title=Infinite series are weird |url=http://skullsinthestars.com/2010/05/25/infinite-series-are-weird-redux/ |first=Greg |last=Gbur |authorlink=Greg Gbur |date=25 May 2010 |website=Skulls in the Stars |accessdate=20 January 2014}}</ref> i.e. the partial sums do not converge to this value, which is denoted by the symbol {{tmath| (\mathfrak{R}) }}. In particular, the <math>(\mathfrak{R})</math> sum of {{nowrap|[[1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ···]]}} was calculated as:
: <math>1+2+3+\cdots = -\frac{1}{12} \quad (\mathfrak{R})</math>

Extending to positive even powers, this gave:
: <math>1 + 2^{2k} + 3^{2k} + \cdots = 0\quad (\mathfrak{R})</math>
and for odd powers the approach suggested a relation with the [[Bernoulli number]]s:
: <math>1+2^{2k-1}+3^{2k-1}+\cdots = -\frac{B_{2k}}{2k}\quad (\mathfrak{R})</math>

It has been proposed to use of ''C''(1) rather than ''C''(0) as the result of Ramanujan's summation, since then it can be assured that one series <math>\textstyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f(k) </math> admits one and only one Ramanujan's summation, defined as the value in 1 of the only solution of the difference equation <math>R(x) - R(x + 1) = f(x)</math> that verifies the condition {{tmath|1= \textstyle \int_1^2 R(t)\,dt = 0 }}.<ref>{{cite book |first=Éric |last=Delabaere |chapter-url=http://algo.inria.fr/seminars/sem01-02/delabaere2.pdf |chapter=Ramanujan's Summation |title=Algorithms Seminar 2001–2002| editor-first=F. |editor-last=Chyzak |publisher=INRIA |year=2003 |pages=83–88}}</ref>

This demonstration of Ramanujan's summation (denoted as <math>\textstyle\sum_{n \ge 1}^{\mathfrak{R}} f(n)</math>) does not coincide with the earlier defined Ramanujan's summation, ''C''(0), nor with the summation of convergent series, but it has interesting properties, such as: If ''R''(''x'') tends to a finite limit when ''x''&nbsp;→&nbsp;1, then the series <math>\textstyle\sum_{n \ge 1}^{\mathfrak{R}} f(n)</math> is convergent, and we have
: <math>\sum_{n \ge 1}^{\mathfrak{R}} f(n) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \left[\sum_{n = 1}^{N}f(n) - \int_1^N f(t)\,dt\right]</math>

In particular, we have
: <math>\sum_{n \ge 1}^\mathfrak{R} \frac{1}{n} = \gamma</math>
where <math>\gamma</math> is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].

== Extension to integrals ==

Ramanujan resummation can be extended to integrals; for example, using the Euler–Maclaurin summation formula, one can write
: <math>\begin{align}
\int_a^\infty x^{m-s} \, dx &= \frac{m-s}{2} \int_a^\infty  \, dx + \zeta (s-m)-\sum_{i=1}^a \left[i^{m-s} +a^{m-s}\right]\\
&\qquad -\sum_{r=1}^\infty \frac{B_{2r} \theta (m-s+1)}{(2r)!\Gamma (m-2r+2-s)} (m-2r+1-s) \int_a^\infty x^{m-2r-s} \, dx 
\end{align}</math>
which is the natural extension to integrals of the zeta regularization algorithm.

This recurrence equation is finite, since for {{tmath| m-2r < -1 }},
: <math>\int_a^\infty dx \, x^{m-2r}= -\frac{a^{m-2r+1}}{m-2r+1} .</math>

Note that this involves (see ''{{slink|Renormalization#Zeta function regularization}}'')
: <math>I(n, \Lambda) = \int_0^\Lambda dx \, x^n .</math>

With {{tmath| \Lambda \to \infty }}, the application of this Ramanujan resummation lends to finite results in the [[renormalization]] of [[quantum field theories]].
